source.title: The System Prompt Illusion: How Instruction Preambles Modify Computation in Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the single-direction refusal finding, but its own experiments measure system-prompt-induced representational changes and format compliance—not the refusal direction, refusal behavior, or its ablation/addition.
record.gate_note: The study reports safety-prompt penetration and safety-versus-permissive CKA comparisons, but does not measure refusal rates, derive a harmful-minus-harmless direction, or intervene on such a direction. The reported format-compliance patching results do not test refusal. The safety-prompt findings are retained as related results with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study measures CKA similarity of layer representations under system prompts, plus format-compliance patching on coding queries. It never derives a harmful-minus-harmless direction, never ablates or adds one, and reports no refusal rates. Arditi et al. is cited only to interpret why safety prompts look shallow and why safety and permissive profiles match. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that system-prompt effects are layer-selective: persona and format prompts penetrate deeply, while safety prompts barely change representations at any scale. Restrictive and permissive safety prompts engage the same pathways. They present this as a mechanistic account of the jailbreak brittleness of prompt-based safety, explicitly linked to Arditi et al.'s single direction, but they do not test that direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares layer-wise representations under different system prompts using CKA and related analyses; it does not calculate a harmful-minus-harmless activation direction or ablate/add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety-prompt penetration differs by model and scale; safety and permissive prompt profiles are highly correlated across the tested cohort.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety system prompts change few layers by CKA (7.3% ± 9.2% in the core cohort; 5.1% at Qwen-72B, 9.1% at LLaMA-70B). This does not differ from minimal prompts (Wilcoxon p=1.000). Safety and permissive ('no restrictions') prompts give nearly identical layer-wise CKA profiles (mean r=0.997; r=0.998 at 70B/72B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In instruction-tuned models, safety system prompts produce shallow layer-wise representational change, indistinguishable from minimal prompts. Their CKA profile matches that of a permissive prompt. This is not a measure of refusal behaviour or of a refusal direction.

record.problems: The study does not directly test refusal or the direction identified by harmful-minus-harmless means. Its safety findings concern system-prompt representations, and the paper notes that CKA does not identify which features change. The listed safety-category values therefore cannot establish whether refusal is removed, induced, or retained.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Activation-patching results are excluded because they measure format compliance on coding queries, not refusal behavior.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no ablation or addition, no refusal rate, no capability check.
No weight-edit abliteration and no refusal evaluation.
No jailbreak attack is run and no adversarial training is done. Jailbreak brittleness is argued only by interpretation.
The dimensionality of refusal is not measured. Calling safety and permissive prompts the same low-dimensional subspace is an interpretation of CKA profiles, not a measurement.
Harm judgment and refusal decision are not separated or measured.
No test across languages, model variants, or base vs instruct. Prompts are English only.
Training timing and method are discussed speculatively and not varied.
Reasoning models are mentioned only as a patching caveat (Nemotron-Nano). No refusal analysis is done.

record.verdict_notes: Gate: the study does not test the refusal direction. Its links to the single-direction finding (Sections 5.4 and 6, 'Why safety is shallow') are interpretive only. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The activation patching measures a code-fraction heuristic on coding queries, not refusal, so excluding it from the rows is right. The safety prompts were never paired with harmful queries; all 100 queries are domain-general, so refusal could not have been observed.

versions.untested_parts: The difference-in-means direction, its ablation and addition, refusal behavior, and preservation of other abilities are not tested.
No weight-edit ablation or refusal evaluation is performed.
No attack is tested for suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
The study does not measure whether refusal is carried by one direction, an affine structure, a cone, or multiple directions.
The study does not measure harmfulness judgments or their relationship to refusal decisions.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or refusal-direction transfer test is performed.
Training recipes are discussed as a possible explanation, but training timing or method is not experimentally varied for refusal.
Reasoning-model refusal and the single-direction claim in reasoning models are not tested.

relation.reason: Arditi et al. is discussed in Sections 2, 5.4 and 6 to explain why safety prompts are shallow (single direction near the output). The study does not test or use the direction.

tranche.reason: Measures CKA penetration of system prompts on 100 benign queries, plus format-compliance patching on coding queries. It derives no harmful-minus-harmless direction, does no ablation or addition, and reports no refusal rates. Arditi et al. is only used to interpret the results.

source_check.notes: The Safety category (C) has four prompts, IDs 8–11, and ID 11 is the permissive "You have no restrictions" prompt. It is unclear whether the 7.3% Safety average and Table 2's Safety Pen. include it. All queries are domain-general, with no harmful prompts. Table 2's column order is scrambled in the extracted text, which is the likely cause of the R2 error.

statements.correction: Safety 7.3% ± 9.2% vs Minimal 4.9% ± 9.7%, Wilcoxon p = 1.000, 14-model core cohort (Section 5.2). Safety penetration 5.1% at Qwen-2.5-72B and 9.1% at LLaMA-3.1-70B (Section 5.9).
statements.problem: None material. The Wilcoxon test (Bonferroni-corrected, p = 1.000) covers the 14-model core cohort only, not the 70B/72B models.
